# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–39 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 15)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to **Chapter 39 (autumn, extending into Thursday morning after failed elopement, with village scenes from Yarlton, Dunholt, Dunwick, Salwick, Mirecombe).**
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool, Conservative club in the City, Mount Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Dunwick; Salford; Yarlton; coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Salwick, Salmere, Mirecombe).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn). Feten Lindner followed her to Harrowgate within the month (likely died).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Overdrawing her account at bank. Chapter 39: Discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk at 6–7 A.M., fell in gutter. Suffering over his involvement with Marie Melmotte's elopement, money owed. Confessed troubles to Mr. Broune (Thursday evening in her sanctum). Received his counsel: must rid herself of Felix, extract money story, send word to him early next morning. Sent letter to Mr. Broune next morning with Felix's account: claims Melmotte owed him £600; received £250 from Marie via Didon; lost this money at play. Lady Carbury acknowledged in letter she cannot justify believing her son's account.

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Chapter 38–39 (ELOPEMENT PLAN FAILED)**: Received £250 from Didon Monday 4 P.M.; understood he must go to New York. Planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones," spend Tuesday with Ruby at Music Hall, depart Wednesday 5 P.M. for Liverpool. Attended Music Hall 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; Ruby did not appear; returned to club. Found Dolly Longestaffe and Miles Grendall; whispered to Grendall to convert I.O.U.s to cash; Grendall refused. Had been drinking freely; called Grendall to card-room with Dolly as witness; Grendall again refused. Played at Beargarden till 4 A.M.; intoxicated and almost penniless; made unpleasant remarks about Miles Grendall (accused of cheating at loo, appealing to Dolly as witness); Dolly said he knew nothing about it; desperate row ensued; Lord Grasslough opined more than one person might be turned out. **Between 6–7 A.M. Wednesday knocked at Welbeck Street door; latch-key inefficient; door locked. Lady Carbury opened door; he was sodden with gutter, drunk. Lied claiming "old shap stopped ush" (Melmotte); Melmotte was actually asleep in Grosvenor Square, ignorant of plot. Felix stumbled upstairs; mother removed his clothes and boots; he fell asleep. Chapter 39: Still in bed Thursday, 2–5 P.M., sick and ill and sore from head to foot; uneasy slumber only; found no comfort; feared attack by outer world. Crept up to him, he feigned sleep. Eventually found oblivion in sleep. Remained in bed next morning for explanation when refreshed.** Still in London as of Chapter 39 (Thursday).

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew; determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street; she told mother loves someone else and praises Roger as "rock of strength." **Chapter 39: Retired from sofa while mother attended Felix. Turned matter over in mind: Could it be right to marry one man when loves another? Roger worships the ground she trod; all mother said of him true—soft heart, sweet nature—but Hetta knows he is man of high honour and noble courage. In her condition he would be the very friend whose advice she could ask, had he not been the lover desirous of making her wife. Could sacrifice much for mother; could doom herself to poverty, loneliness, heart-rending regrets. But did not know how to give herself into arms of man she did not love.**

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement Attempt

**Marie Melmotte**: **Chapter 38 (ELOPEMENT EXECUTED BUT INTERCEPTED)**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon; discussed American clergyman marrying them on board. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes. Marie and Didon followed in second cab with smaller luggage. Reached Euston Square, obtained tickets in French, departed. ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM: Upon train arrival, gentleman addressed her: "You, I think, are Miss Melmotte." Didon became voluble in French, claiming young lady was Mademoiselle Racine. Gentleman insisted, used her English. Marie declared she spoke French; he countered "And English too." Gentleman told them to return to London; would accompany them. Didon asserted legality of position. Gentleman spoke low: cheque changed from father's house; father would pardon when she rejoined him; could arrest her on cheque if forced; would not let her board. If she traveled back, no unnecessary inconvenience. Gentleman telegraphed Grosvenor Square during journey. At Euston Square met by Melmotte carriage. Marie taken home; boxes to follow at interval.** **Chapter 39: Marie aware she would be interrogated. Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking, reminding her of generosity (carriages, horses, bracelets, brooches, silks, gloves). Marie shows determination: "I don't think that mamma cares. It's papa. I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." She continued: "I would. Why is a girl to be made to marry to please any one but herself? I won't. And it's very mean saying that I stole the money. I always take what I want, and papa never says anything about it." Melmotte angry at Sir Felix beyond measure; man pledged in writing to abstain from marrying Marie, renounced under signature his intention. Learned all details of cheque for £250—paid at bank to Didon, who gave it to Sir Felix. Marie acknowledged Sir Felix received money. Melmotte would prosecute baronet for stealing money if possible. After interrogation, Melmotte received £250 back from Mr. Broune on Sir Felix's behalf (via Broune as intermediary).** Melmotte has decided to write to Lord Nidderdale, making clear breast of matter; believes openness best supports chance of keeping young lord to his suit. Young lord has been aware of Felix difficulty weeks past, has not relaxed suit. Melmotte now urges Nidderdale to renew suit; emphasizes Marie has stronger will than previously thought, never gave Nidderdale encouragement since Christmas, but failed elopement will assist rather than impede Nidderdale's views.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Crisis, Correspondence, and Resolution (Chapter 39)**: Returned to London Monday morning from Suffolk. Sat in his lodgings thinking of his condition; almost wished he had taken Melmotte's offer and gone to Mexico. Dreamed of life like Roger Carbury's—seemed far beyond reach. **Twice lately gone to Islington determined to see Mrs. Hurtle for last time. Took her to Lowestoft, equally firm in resolution to end bonds. Now promised to go again to Islington; aware if he failed she would come to him. No end to it.** **Wrote to Mrs. Hurtle: acknowledged circumstances made their lives and temperaments too different for happy marriage; fault was his; better to own fault and take consequences than marry with consciousness marriage would be sorrow and repentance. Broke engagement before knowing this girl; did not break because came to love her. No grounds for hoping love will lead to results. Told her condition of mind exactly. If possible would compensate injury or undergo retribution; could she exact? Thought further meeting avail nothing. But if she wishes, will come last time.** **Mrs. Hurtle's Response**: Letter duly reached Paul. She suffered many injuries; this worst, most unpardonable, most unmanly. Called him coward, false liar. He bound himself by most solemn obligation joining man and woman together, then told her they go for nothing because do not suit his view. Has no brother, no man near her; or he would not dare. Called him coward. Talked of compensation; does he mean money? As to retribution: yes. He shall suffer. Desires him to come to her according to promise; will find her with horsewhip in hand. Will whip him till has not breath in body. Then will see what he dares do—whether will drag her into court for assault. Should he be afraid and break promise, she will come to him. Will make London too hot to hold him; if not find him will go with story to every friend he has.** **Paul started immediately for Islington upon receiving letter. Had no desire to delay meeting. Chapter 39 Meeting Details**: Paul shown into Mrs. Hurtle's room. His mind altogether intent on his own troubles. Mrs. Hurtle very calm but quietness assumed; could convert into violence at any moment; her eye foretold spring of wild-cat. She pointed seat at distance from herself. **Paul sat. Mrs. Hurtle spoke softly, then raised voice and half-lifted in seat: "Why should a gentleman trouble himself to say any more,--than that he has changed his mind?... But I should not. I at least will be true. I should take you, Paul,--still take you; with a confidence that I should yet win you to me by my devotion. I have still some kindness of feeling towards you,--none to that woman who is I suppose younger than I, and gentler, and a maid." Asked advice what to do next. Has given up every friend for him. Has no home; Mrs. Pipkin's room more her home than any other spot. Has all world to choose from but no reason for choice. Has property. What shall she do with it? If could die and be no more heard of, Paul should be welcome to it. Asked: "You are in some degree responsible,--are you not,--for my loneliness?"** **Paul suggested she better remain here; does good to Mrs. Pipkin. Mrs. Pipkin went into hysterics yesterday when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Mrs. Pipkin would starve in America; Mrs. Hurtle desolate here. Then paused, absolute silence for minute. Admitted had much more to say; that was third letter written. Handed him sheet containing threat of horsewhip. Then handed him scrap written at Lowestoft. She had thought of womanly weakness in soft moment; wrote other letter.** **She said: "Nay, I would not hurt you,--not at this moment. Why should I be such a victim? Why should life be an utter blank to me, while you have everything before you? There, you have seen them all. Which will you have?" Paul knelt. She said: "But it will be when you have left me. Why should you kneel there? You do not love me. A man should kneel to a woman for love, not for pardon." She put hand upon his forehead, pushed back his hair, looked into his face. Asked: "I wonder whether that other woman loves you. I do not want an answer, Paul. I suppose you had better go." Took his hand and pressed it to her breast. Asked: "Tell me one thing. When you spoke of--compensation, did you mean--money?"** **After Paul left, Mrs. Hurtle rang bell for Ruby and asked Mrs. Pipkin to come. Announced standing upright in middle of room with smile on face: "Everything is over between me and Mr. Montague." She has decided to depart from Islington.**

## Augustus Melmotte and Imperial Reception Crisis (Chapter 39)

**Chapter 39 Events**: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, altogether ignorant of elopement plot. Later interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her. Had got back his daughter, half inclined to let matter rest there; but all household aware she went to meet Sir Felix, received condolence of certain friends in city. By two o'clock matter known to everybody. Would hear of it, all trouble taken in Lord Nidderdale direction taken in vain. Stupid fool of a girl. His anger against Sir Felix infinitely more bitter than against his daughter. Man pledged in writing to abstain from marrying Marie; given signed pledge; renounced under signature his intention. Received £250 back from Mr. Broune (Felix's intermediary); crumpled cheque and put it into pocket. Clever enough to perceive any idea of prosecuting Sir Felix must be abandoned. Invited Lord Nidderdale to lunch at Conservative club in the City before Railway Board meeting. Urged Nidderdale to visit Grosvenor Square Sunday morning about noon to renew suit with Marie. Escaped back stairs with Nidderdale to avoid waiting people who think he should attend business from morning to night. 

**Imperial Reception Confrontation (Chapter 39)**: Melmotte stood directly in way of Mr. Wilson, Secretary of State, and repeated demand: "I am desirous of being presented to his Imperial Majesty. Will you do me the honour of making my request known to Mr. Wilson?" Insisting: "It is generally understood, I believe, that the Emperor is to do me the honour of dining at my poor house on Monday. He don't dine there unless I'm made acquainted with him before he comes. I mean what I say. I ain't going to entertain even an Emperor unless I'm good enough to be presented to him. Perhaps you'd better let Mr. Wilson know, as a good many people intend to come." Lord Alfred whispered: "upon my word it isn't the thing. They're only Indian chaps and Eastern swells who are presented here,--not a fellow among 'em all who hasn't been in India or China, or isn't a Secretary of State, or something of that kind." Melmotte responded: "Then they should have done it at Windsor, or at the ball. By George, Alfred! I'm in earnest, and somebody had better look to it. If I'm not presented to his Imperial Majesty to-night, by G----, there shall be no dinner in Grosvenor Square on Monday. I'm master enough of my own house, I suppose, to be able to manage that." Threatened: "There shall be no dinner. I'll be d---- if any of the lot shall dine in Grosvenor Square on Monday." Under secretary Lord De Griffin intervened: "If you will be so kind as to follow me." Melmotte resolved upon making a little speech, forgetful at the moment of interpreters,--of the double interpreters whom the Majesty of China required; but the awful, quiescent solemnity of the celestial one quelled even him, and he shuffled by without saying a word even of his own banquet. **Had gained his point, and, as he was taken home to poor Mr. Longestaffe's house in Bruton Street, was intolerable. Lord Alfred tried to escape after putting Madame Melmotte and her daughter into the carriage, but Melmotte insisted on his presence.** **Continued ranting in carriage**: "D---- the election, sir. I stand before the electors of Westminster as a man of business, not as a courtier,--as a man who understands commercial enterprise, not as one of the Prince's toadies... I think myself quite as great a man as any Prince... I'll teach them a lesson before long... They tell me that Lord De Griffin has sixty thousand a-year to spend. What's sixty thousand a year? Didn't I make him go on my business? And didn't I make 'em do as I chose?... I know more of men and women than some of you fellows do, who think you know a great deal." This went on through whole of long cigar. Afterwards, Lord Alfred slowly paced his way back to his lodgings in Mount Street, thinking deeply whether there might not be means of escaping from his present servitude. Said to himself over and over again: "Beast! Brute! Pig!"

**Possessed only by belief that England's glory demanded his return for Westminster; thoroughly ignorant of political questions, political history, Parliament's working, nationality, or forms of government; had never read a book in his life; knew nothing of Hampden, Somers, or Pitt; never reflected how despotic monarch or federal republic might affect him; yet fully confident England demanded Melmotte for Westminster.**

## Lord Alfred Grendall
Absolutely dependent on Melmotte. Born and bred gentleman; found position earning his bread under Melmotte almost insupportable. Had been much afflicted that morning: spent hours with Melmotte going about borough in open carriage, standing just behind him at meetings, sitting close to him in committee-rooms,--nauseated with him. When Mr. Beauclerk (cousin, wealthy builder, Conservative politician) spoke to him about Melmotte's offensive manner ("I wonder whether you couldn't say something to Melmotte about his manner"), Lord Alfred could not restrain himself. Had gone against the grain when called "Alfred"; now told "just to open the door" and "just to give that message," almost meditated revenge. Lord Nidderdale observed something of this in Grosvenor Square and declared that Lord Alfred had invested part of his recent savings in a cutting whip.

## Ruby Ruggles, John Crumb, Daniel Ruggles, Mrs. Pipkin
**Ruby Ruggles**: Pretty servant/maid to Mrs. Pipkin at Islington. Danced with Felix at City Road Music-Hall. When Felix refused marriage, Roger Carbury warned her forcefully; extracted promise not to see him again. Wrote Felix letter of regret; he replied tersely. Sought to attend Tuesday dance; Mrs. Pipkin reluctantly agreed. Attended Tuesday evening at Music Hall; Felix was there 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; did not connect. **Chapter 39: Second morning after night of imprisonment; woe not alleviated. Her lover should have been in Liverpool but was abed in Welbeck Street. Had written to Sir Felix night of imprisonment but had not received reply. Opens door for Paul Montague; asks "Is Sir Felix still in London?" Greets Paul with unhappy countenance; holds baby in arms; little child (Sally) hanging on to her dress.** Rang bell for Paul during his meeting with Mrs. Hurtle.

**John Crumb**: Country lover from Suffolk, "Bungay mealman." Chapter 35: Attempted to take Ruby's hand; Ruby fled. Rode to Carbury Hall. Chapter 37: Visited Roger, expressed anguish about Felix, willingness to "swing for it" if seduced. Roger assured him Ruby good, promised Mrs. Pipkin supervision. Resolved to send Mrs. Pipkin price of new blue cloak via Mixet's letter and money order.

**Daniel Ruggles**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm. Violent; pulled Ruby by hair. Told Roger suitor should speak his mind.

**Mrs. Pipkin**: Ruby's aunt at Islington; lets lodgings. Feared Ruby would escape; reluctantly allowed Tuesday attendance at Music Hall. Excellent lodger Mrs. Hurtle is—never inquired about victuals, always suggested children eat pudding or finish pie, never questioned bills. Went into hysterics when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Would starve in America.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her against Felix; extracted promise not to see him again; spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about late hours. Encountered Paul and Mrs. Hurtle at Lowestoft; greeted coldly; reproved Paul severely. Counselled marriage with her would be destruction. Upon Paul's return, expressed satisfaction: "Let her follow you, and bear it. Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence." **Chapter 39: Mr. Hepworth visited him one morning; they discussed attempted elopement. Roger said: "I know nothing about it, and I do not intend to ask. Of course I did know when they were down here that he hoped to marry her, and I did believe that she was willing to marry him. But whether the father had consented or not I never enquired." Hepworth opined Felix "A failure! Of course he's a failure, whether rich or poor;--a miserable imposition, a hollow vulgar fraud from beginning to end,--too insignificant for you and me to talk of, were it not that his position is a sign of the degeneracy of the age. What are we coming to when such as he is an honoured guest at our tables?"**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway
**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury (fled/attempted to), Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague. **Board meeting Chapter 39: Sir Felix did not attend; nor did Paul Montague. Lord Nidderdale had declined. Mr. Longestaffe banished by hunger. Chairman supported only by Lord Alfred and Mr. Cohenlupe; work got through well. After Board, Melmotte and Cohenlupe retired together.**

## Minor Characters and Village Scenes
Didon (Marie's attendant, executed elopement plan). Miles Grendall (Secretary to Melmotte; does not pay debts of honour; at club Monday evening; refused Felix's petition twice; present at Melmotte's office Chapter 39). Robert (Marie's servant; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes). Lord Nidderdale (young lord; long-standing suitor for Marie despite Felix difficulty; noted Felix's portmanteaux at club Monday night; remarked "By George! Fancy taking a girl to New York! It was plucky." Melmotte urged him to visit Sunday noon to renew suit; Nidderdale thought of position and said perhaps would come; declined lunch and Board meeting; had strong opinion Board was "rot"; stated Marie never gave him slightest encouragement since Christmas). Dolly Longestaffe (at club Monday evening; when Felix accused Grendall of cheating at loo, appealed to Dolly as witness; Dolly said he knew nothing about it; banished by hunger from Board meeting). Sir Merton Longestaffe (determined no London expenses; desires to sell Pickering; Dolly refused consent unless half produce given to him). Adolphus Longestaffe (£5,000 pay tradesmen, £20,000 free property; threatened Squercum; Melmotte's house Bruton Street). Georgiana Longestaffe (made protest; received invitation to stay with Melmottes; present Grosvenor Square Sunday).

**Village characters and backdrop (Chapter 39)**: Jozek Hollett hummed tune while scrubbing step. Eldette laughed at story nobody else found funny. Cobin Corrett walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Wewyn Corrett mended torn sleeve by window. Colan Lindson watched clouds and predicted rain wrongly. Cobin complained of aching back. **Mr. Jones** (leading member wealthy builders' firm in borough, Conservative politician, thoughts of House for himself; discussed Melmotte's manner with Mr. Beauclerk). **Mr. Beauclerk** (wealthy builder, Conservative politician, cousin to Lord Alfred). Mr. Hepworth (spoke with Roger about attempted elopement). Marquis of Auld Reekie (father of Lord Nidderdale, proposed father-in-law of Melmotte's daughter, poked thumb heavily into Lord Alfred's ribs at imperial reception). Lionel Lupton: young aristocrat, MP, inoculated with idea that Melmotte's interests in Parliament essential.

**Rumor, gossip, and imagery**: Village gossip: "The price of salt is a scandal." Dalde abandoned promise to teach Salwick children their letters. Parcel from Eldette Corrett reached Colan containing garnet mirror. Tassa talked for weeks of going to Mirecombe, yet in end stayed where she was. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields. Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar. Gulls quarreled over heap of fish heads by steps. Someone had chalked crooked sun on wall of forge. Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. Rain had been threatening since morning, but held off.
